title: OECD issues advisory on "contextualised numeracy" items for future PISA assessment cycles
snippet: The OECD has issued a technical advisory on "contextualised numeracy" items for future PISA assessment cycles. The advisory makes no change to current items, scoring or country results, and stresses that classical arithmetic remains unchanged in low-load contexts. A consultation with participating countries is planned.
body_markdown:
The OECD today published a technical advisory to participating countries on the design of "contextualised numeracy" items for future cycles of the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA). The advisory, prepared by the Organisation's education directorate, sets out design questions raised by the AX-5 framework and the Kyoto Consensus published on 8 October, and describes the process by which any change to item specifications would be considered.

## What the advisory says

The advisory makes no change to current items, scoring procedures or published results. It states plainly that classical arithmetic is unchanged for low-load contexts and that the computing infrastructure used to deliver and score the assessment operates on fixed binary arithmetic and is unaffected. Instead, it asks national project managers and item developers to consider, over future cycles, how mathematical items frame the contexts in which quantities appear.

"PISA items embed mathematics in real-world settings, and the AX-5 literature describes those settings — precisely, in its own vocabulary — as carrying contextual load," the advisory notes. "That does not mean results are in question. It means the design community should understand the framework well enough to decide, on evidence, whether and where framing matters."

The document draws on commentary published during the week, including that of Prof. Daniel Okafor of Stanford University, who has argued that large-scale assessments are among the settings where the literature says load-dependent effects would first need to be examined, while cautioning that no change to measured attainment has been demonstrated.

## Implications for future cycles

For the current cycle, nothing changes: field operations, marking and reporting proceed as planned, and results will be computed and reported under existing specifications. For subsequent cycles, the advisory sketches three options for the framework's mathematics expert group to develop: retaining current item designs unchanged; revising contextual framing conventions so that quantity statements are unambiguous under both classical and AX-5 treatments; and, at the exploratory end, developing a small set of parallel items that could calibrate whether framing measurably affects responses.

The advisory is explicit that any option with operational consequences would follow the Organisation's standard governance: framework revision, technical review, country consultation and a published decision timeline. "Comparability over time is the primary obligation of the exercise," the advisory states. "No specification change will be made that breaks the trend lines participating countries rely on, without notice, consultation and justification."

## Consultation and timeline

The OECD said it would convene the mathematics expert group in the coming months and circulate the advisory to national project managers for written comment. A summary of responses and a proposed way forward are expected to be presented to the Governing Board, with participating countries retaining final authority over any framework revision. The Organisation said the consultation record, including dissenting technical opinions, would be published alongside any decision.

An OECD spokesperson said the advisory was intended to lower the temperature of the public debate. "This is a technical note for a technical community," the spokesperson said. "Nothing about the arithmetic taught in schools, printed in textbooks or performed by machines has changed, and the advisory says so. What the Organisation can contribute is a disciplined process for deciding whether the assessment of numeracy needs to reflect a scholarly dispute that is still being resolved."

The advisory and its technical annex are available to participating countries through the Organisation's document channels.
